Essential medspa SOPs and implementation templates
That is a strong revenue machine. What is comparatively thin is the cost and economics side, which is the half of the equation that actually decides whether all that revenue becomes profit. For a question framed specifically around profitability, that is where the real gaps are.

Here is where I would build next, in priority order.

1. **The Profit and Numbers Playbook.** This is the single biggest hole and the one I would build first. Most med spa owners are clinicians who can read a face but not a profit and loss statement. This playbook would teach an owner to run the practice by the numbers: target net margin, labor cost ratio, cost of goods per service, owner pay, and the handful of weekly and monthly figures that predict profit before the bank account confirms it. Every other playbook you own grows revenue. This is the only one that tells an owner whether that revenue is actually turning into money they keep. It also strengthens your core offer, because it lets you promise profitable growth, not just growth.

2. **The Compensation and Incentive Playbook.** Labor is usually the largest line item in a med spa, and provider pay, especially injector pay, is where margin quietly disappears. This would give owners model structures (base versus commission, tiered, team bonus tied to practice metrics), realistic benchmarks, and the harder piece, how to transition existing staff onto a healthier structure without losing them. High leverage and a true gap. I would consider building it right alongside number one, since together they own the entire cost side your library does not currently touch.

3. **The Pricing and Menu Engineering Playbook.** You already do profitability audits against wholesale cost on a case by case basis. This systematizes that into a repeatable method: price every service to a target margin, then shape the menu toward high margin and high capacity services and away from the loss leaders owners keep out of habit. It extends your Package Architecture work, but from the cost up rather than the offer down.

4. **The Capacity and Scheduling Playbook.** Once fixed costs are covered, every additional filled chair or room is almost pure margin, and almost no owner optimizes this. This would cover provider utilization targets, booking density, scheduling rules, and how to shrink idle time. It is one of the most overlooked profit levers in the industry.

5. **The Acquisition Economics Playbook.** You have ad playbooks for Jacques and organic for Keisha, but those are operator facing. This is the owner facing companion that answers what a client is actually worth, what they can afford to spend to acquire one, the payback period, and how to choose between channels. It connects marketing spend to profit so owners stop guessing at ad budgets.</untrusted_external_data></chat>

A few decisions worth knowing about:

**On the library one-pager.** I gave each item a one-line description rather than listing names alone. A bare list of thirty titles reads like a table of contents and a prospect cannot tell what any of it does. I left out the internal-only assets (Setter Playbook, SOP Standards and Master Index are yours, not theirs) except the SOP index, which I kept because clients do receive a version of it. The Case Study Library is listed as sales support, which is slightly odd on a client-facing sheet, so cut that line if it reads wrong to you.

**On the two-pager.** Page one is the two real case studies with the video quotes underneath. Page two is the six written testimonials in a two-up grid, then the CTA, then your site's results disclaimer verbatim.

Two things I'd flag as the weakest points:

The eleven-study case study library is the obvious thing to put in a proof document, and I deliberately did not. Six of those eleven are illustrative composites rather than measured client results, and putting fabricated dollar figures on the same page as named, verifiable testimonials is where credibility risk concentrates. If you want depth on page two, the stronger move is adding the New Jersey two-location example from the Aesthetic Renewal proposal, since that one you can substantiate.

Mike's numbers are the only hard figures in the document and they come from your own site copy. If those came from the client rather than from your reporting, get them confirmed in writing before this goes out at volume. The specificity is what makes the page work, and it is also what a skeptical prospect will ask you to back up.

1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:
    10	
    11	| Task | Approach |
    12	|---|---|
    13	| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
    14	| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
    15	| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |
    16	
    17	> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.
    18	
    19	## Creating with docx-js — gotchas
    20	
    21	`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:
    22	
    23	- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
    24	- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
    25	- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
    26	- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
    27	- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
    28	- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
    29	- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
    30	- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
    31	- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
    32	- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
    33	- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.
    34	
    35	## Verify the output
    36	
    37	After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:
    38	
    39	```bash
    40	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
    41	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
    42	ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
    43	```
    44	
    45	`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).
    46	
    47	## Editing existing documents
    48	
    49	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.
    50	
    51	```bash
    52	unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
    53	find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
    54	python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
    55	# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
    56	(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)
    57	python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
    58	# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
    59	```
    60	
    61	Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).

A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. content.text:
Rebuilt. The document is now 8 pages: featured story, eleven case studies, testimonials, aggregate impact, and a closing page.

What I removed per your instruction: the opening two-part explanation, the "Premium Tier: Practices at $2.5M and Above" header and its lead-in, and the "Foundational Results: Growth-Stage Practices" header and its lead-in. The studies now run 01 through 11 in one sequence with no tiering. I also pulled the revenue qualifiers out of the Practice Type lines, so study one reads "Multi-Provider Medical Spa" rather than "Multi-Provider Medical Spa, $2.5M annual revenue." Same logic: that line was doing the same gating work the headers were.

Three other calls I made:

Mike's spotlight came off page one because he is case study 07. Running the same story twice in eight pages reads sloppy, so his video quote now sits inside study 07 instead. Lisa Bell stays as the featured story since she is not in the eleven. Olivia's quote got attached to study 10 the same way.

I renamed study 10 from "Secret Shopper Review" to "Confidential Experience Assessment" so it matches what you actually sell.

Aggregate impact moved to after the testimonials, and I used your bottom-line copy as the closing section so the last page is a real close rather than a stranded CTA.

Two weak points:

**Studies 01 through 06 now sit in the same numbered sequence as your real ones.** Rebecca M., Jonathan R., Stephanie K., Catherine D., Marisa L., and Andrea T. are composites with invented dollar figures. Mike, Megan, Danielle, Olivia, and Emily are real people whose names appear on your testimonials page. In this document a prospect cannot tell which is which, and neither could opposing counsel if a client ever claimed they were sold on results that never happened. The results-vary disclaimer covers variation in outcomes. It does not cover attributed outcomes that did not occur. The clean fix is either a short line marking 01 through 06 as illustrative models of the systems, or replacing them with real numbers as you accumulate them.

**Study 03's headline still says "Scaled From $2.5M Toward $3.4M."** You just asked me to strip the who-it-is-for signals, and that title puts one right back at the top of the page. A $700K owner reads it and quietly decides this document is not about her. Retitling it around the mechanism, something like "Connected the Pieces Into a System and Grew 36 Percent Without Adding Locations," keeps the number in the body where it belongs as proof rather than as a filter.
